en: Thus have I heard— Majjhima Nikāya 25, the Nivāpa Sutta (The Bait).
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, it is not the case that a deer-trapper sets out bait for the various kinds of deer:”
‘May these deer, while consuming this bait laid out by me, live long, be beautiful, and endure for a long time.
And so, monks, the bait-layer lays out the bait for the deer, thinking:
‘Having crowded around this bait laid out by me, the deer will become infatuated and consume the food; having crowded around it—’
"Intoxicated by eating these foods, they will become intoxicated; being intoxicated, they will fall into negligence;
being negligent, they will come under the power of the hunter to do with them as he pleases in this baited trap.
Therein, monks, the first group of deer did not approach that bait laid out by the hunter.
They ate the food with infatuation; while eating the food there, having intruded upon it, they fell into intoxication.
Being intoxicated, they fell into heedlessness; being heedless, they became subject to the hunter’s doing as he wished regarding that bait.
"Thus, monks, those first deer were not released from the power of the hunter's supernatural influence.
Thereupon, monks, the second group of deer reflected thus:
'Those first deer who, having approached that bait laid out by the hunter, ate their food while infatuated with it—'"

There, having crowded together and become infatuated while eating their food, they fell into intoxication; being intoxicated, they fell into negligence; and being negligent, they became subject to the hunter’s doing as he wished regarding that bait.
Thus, those first species of deer were not released from the power of the hunter’s supernatural influence.
"What if we were to abstain entirely from the bait-food? Having abstained from the enjoyment of fear, let us plunge into the forest wilds and dwell there."
They completely abstained from eating bait; having abstained from fear and enjoyment, they dwelt having plunged deep into forest retreats.
In the last month of summer, when grass and water were exhausted, their bodies reached a state of extreme emaciation.
As their bodies reached that state of extreme emaciation, their strength and energy declined.
When their strength and vigor had failed, they returned to that very same bait set by the trapper.
Having intruded there, they became infatuated and ate the food.

While eating the food there, having intruded and become infatuated, they fell into intoxication; being intoxicated, they fell into negligence; and being negligent, they became subject to the trapper’s doing with that bait as he wished.
"Thus, monks, even the second generation of deer was not released from the power of the hunter's supernatural influence.
Then, monks, the third generation of deer reflected thus:
'Those first deer who [ate] that bait laid out by the hunter...'"
For thus those first deer did not escape from the power of the hunter's supernatural influence.
And as for those second deer who thought thus:
"Those first deer who [ate] that bait laid down by the hunter... [and so on].
"Thus indeed those first deer of the herd were not released from the power of the snare-setter's supernatural influence.
Suppose we were to abstain entirely from the bait-food; having abstained from the enjoyment of fear, let us enter deep into the forest wilds and dwell there.
They abstained entirely from the bait-food; having abstained from the enjoyment of fear, they entered deep into the forest wilds and dwelt there.
In the last month of summer, when grass and water were exhausted, their bodies reached a state of extreme exhaustion.
As their bodies reached this state of extreme exhaustion, their strength and energy declined.
When their strength and energy had declined, they returned to that very same bait laid out by the hunter.
There they intruded upon one another and, being infatuated, ate the food.

While eating the food there, having intruded upon one another and being infatuated, they fell into intoxication; being intoxicated, they fell into negligence; and being negligent, they became subject to whatever the deer-trapper wished to do with that bait.
Thus, for a second time, those species of deer were not released from the power of the deer-trapper’s success.
"Perhaps we might make our dwelling in dependence upon that bait laid out by the fowler.
Having made our dwelling there, we shall eat the food laid out as bait by the fowler without encroaching upon it and without becoming infatuated;
eating the food without encroaching upon it and without becoming infatuated, we shall not fall into intoxication; being unintoxicated—"
“Being heedful, we shall not fall into negligence; being heedful, we shall not become subject to the hunter’s will regarding that bait.
Relying upon that bait laid out by the hunter, they established their dwelling nearby.
Having established their dwelling there, they ate the food provided by the hunter without encroaching upon it and without becoming infatuated with it.
They ate there, not encroaching upon one another and remaining uninfatuated while eating their food;
they did not fall into intoxication. Being sober, they did not fall into negligence. Being diligent, they did not become subject to the hunter's will regarding that bait.
In this regard, monks, it occurred to the deer-trapper and his retinue:
“These third deer are indeed cunning and deceptive; these third deer are indeed powerful and capable of outwitting others.
They consume this bait that has been laid down, yet we do not know their coming or their going.”
“Perhaps we should surround this bait that has been laid out on all sides with large nets, so that we might see the third group of deer’s lair where they go to take the bait.
They then surrounded that laid-out bait on all sides with large nets.
Monks, the baiter and his retinue saw the third group of deer’s lair where they went to take the bait.
In this way, monks, even those third deer were not released from the power of the hunter’s supernatural might.
Then, monks, the fourth deer reflected thus: “Those first deer... [as before] ...”
For thus those first deer were not released from the power of the hunter’s supernatural might.
And as for those second deer who thought thus:
“Those first deer... [as before]...”
"In this way, those first deer of the herd were not released from the power of the snare-setter’s supernatural influence.
What if we were to abstain entirely from the bait-food? Having abstained from the enjoyment of fear, let us plunge into the forest wilderness and dwell there.
They abstained entirely from the bait-food... [and so on]...
In this way, even those second deer were not released from the power of the hunter’s supernatural influence.
And as for those third deer who thought thus:
“Those first deer... [as before]...”
For thus those first deer were not released from the power of the hunter’s supernatural might.
And as for those second deer who thought thus:
“Those first deer... [as before]...”
"In this way, those first deer of the herd were not liberated from the power of the hunter's snare.
Suppose we were to abstain entirely from the bait-food; abstaining from the enjoyment of fear, let us plunge into the forest wilderness and dwell there.
They abstained entirely from the bait-food... [as before]...
"In this way, even those second deer were not released from the power of the hunter's snare.
Suppose we were to establish our dwelling near that bait laid out by the hunter;
having established our dwelling there, we shall eat our food without encroaching upon that bait laid out by the hunter and without becoming infatuated with it."
“By eating our food without encroaching on others and without becoming infatuated, we shall not fall into intoxication;
being free from intoxication, we shall not fall into negligence; and being diligent, we shall not become subject to the hunter’s will regarding that bait.
They made their dwelling near that bait laid out by the hunter, and having established their dwelling there—
They ate the food set out as bait by the deer-trapper without encroaching upon it and without becoming infatuated;
eating there without encroaching or being infatuated, they did not fall into intoxication;
being sober, they did not fall into negligence; and being heedful, they did not become subject to the trapper’s will regarding that bait.
Then it occurred to the deer-trapper and his retinue:

“These third deer are indeed crafty and deceptive; these third deer are indeed powerful and belong to another species, for they consume this very bait that has been laid out, yet we do not know their coming or their going.”

"Suppose we were to surround this bait that has been laid down on all sides with large enclosures of stakes, so that we might perhaps see the third group of deer's lair, where they go to take hold of it.
They then surrounded that laid-down bait on all sides with large enclosures of stakes.
And the bait-layer and his retinue saw the third group of deer's lair, where they went to take hold of it.
Thus, even for a third time, those deer did not escape from the power of the hunter's supernatural influence.
"Suppose we were to establish our dwelling in a place where the hunter and his retinue have no access;
having established our dwelling there, let us eat the food provided by the hunter without encroaching upon that bait laid out, and without becoming infatuated."
"We shall eat; eating our food without encroaching [on others] and without being infatuated, we shall not fall into intoxication.
Being free from intoxication, we shall not fall into negligence. Being diligent, we shall not become subject to the hunter's will regarding that bait.
Thus they made their dwelling wherever there was no access for the hunter or his retinue.
Having established their dwelling there, they ate the bait laid out by the deer-trapper without encroaching upon it and without becoming infatuated with it.
While eating those foods there, not encroaching and not being infatuated, they did not fall into intoxication;
being sober, they did not fall into negligence; and being diligent, they did not become subject to the will of others.
“...at that bait laid out by the deer-trapper.
Thereupon, monks, it occurred to the deer-trapper and his retinue:
‘These fourth deer-herds are indeed cunning and deceptive; these fourth deer-herds are indeed powerful and capable of deceiving others.’”
“They are consuming this bait that has been laid out, yet we do not know their coming or their going.
What if we were to surround this laid-out bait on all sides with large nets set in place? Perhaps we might see the lair of the fourth species of deer, where they go to be caught.
So they surrounded that laid-out bait on all sides with large nets set in place.
“Monks, neither the deer-trapper nor his retinue saw the lair of the fourth species of deer where they might go for capture.
Then, monks, it occurred to the deer-trapper and his retinue:
‘If we disturb the fourth species of deer, being disturbed themselves, they will disturb others; being disturbed by them, others will be disturbed.’”
"In this way, all the deer will escape from this bait that has been laid out.
Suppose we were to overlook the fourth kind of deer.
And so, monks, the bait-layer and his retinue overlooked the fourth kind of deer.
"In this way, monks, those fourth deer were released from the power of the hunter's supernormal influence.
Monks, I have told this simile for the purpose of making a point clear.
And this is the meaning here:"
“‘The bait,’ monks, is a designation for the five strands of sensual pleasure.
‘The fisherman,’ monks, is a designation for Māra the Evil One.
‘The fisherman’s retinue,’ monks, is a designation for Māra’s retinue.”
“Migajāta,” monks, is a designation for recluses and brahmins.
Therein, monks, the first recluses and brahmins, having intruded upon that bait set out by Māra and those worldly baits, ate their food with infatuation.
While eating their food there, having intruded and being infatuated, they fell into intoxication; being intoxicated, they—
They fell into negligence; being negligent, they became subject to Māra’s doing as he wished regarding that bait and that worldly lure.
Thus, monks, those first recluses and brahmins were not liberated from Māra’s power and influence.
Monks, I say that these first recluses and brahmins are just like those first species of deer.
In this regard, monks, the second group of recluses and brahmins reflected thus:
“Those first recluses and brahmins, having intruded upon that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly baits, ate their food with infatuation.
While eating their food there, having intruded and being infatuated, they fell into intoxication; being intoxicated, they—”
They fell into negligence; being negligent, they became subject to Māra’s doing as he wished regarding that bait and that worldly lure.
Thus those first recluses and brahmins were not liberated from Māra’s supernormal power.
"What if we were to abstain entirely from that bait-food and worldly lures? Having abstained from the enjoyment of fear, let us enter deep into forest dwellings and live there."
They completely abstained from food consisting of bait and worldly baits; having abstained from the enjoyment of fear, they entered deep into forest regions and dwelt there.
They completely abstained from food consisting of bait and worldly baits; having abstained from the enjoyment of fear, they entered deep into forest regions and dwelt there.
There, they became eaters of herbs, eaters of millet, eaters of wild rice, and eaters of wild beans.
They were eaters of hailstones; they were eaters of grain-husks; they were eaters of scum of boiled rice;
they were eaters of oil-cake; they were eaters of grass; they were eaters of cow-dung; they sustained themselves by subsisting on the roots and fruits of the forest, eating only fallen fruit.
In the last month of summer, when grass and water were exhausted, their bodies reached a state of extreme emaciation.
As their bodies reached the highest degree of emaciation, their strength and energy declined.
When their strength and energy had declined, their liberation of mind declined.
With the decline of their liberation of mind, they returned to that very bait set out by Māra, and to those worldly baits.
There they intruded and, being infatuated, ate their food.
While eating their food there, having intruded and being infatuated, they fell into intoxication; being intoxicated, they fell into negligence;
and being negligent, they became subject to Māra’s doing as he wishes regarding that bait and that worldly lure.
"Thus, monks, for a second time those ascetics and brahmins were not liberated from Māra’s power of psychic influence.
Just as those deer of the second herd, monks, so do I describe these second ascetics and brahmins.
Then, monks, the third ascetics and brahmins reflected thus:"

“Those first recluses and brahmins who [fell for] that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly baits… Thus indeed those first recluses and brahmins were not liberated from the power of Māra’s psychic might.
And as for those second recluses and brahmins who thought thus:”
“Those first recluses and brahmins who [partook] of that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly baits...
Thus indeed those first recluses and brahmins were not liberated from the power of Māra’s psychic might.
Suppose we were to abstain entirely from that bait-food and worldly baits; being free from the enjoyment of fear, let us enter deep into the forest dwellings and dwell there.”
They completely abstained from all food consisting of bait and worldly baits.
Having abstained from fear and enjoyment, they entered deep into forest regions and dwelt there.
There, they became eaters of herbs... [and so on] ...living on windfallen fruits.
In the last month of summer, when grass and water were exhausted, their bodies reached a state of extreme exhaustion.
As their bodies reached this extreme exhaustion, their strength and energy declined; with their strength and energy declined, their liberation of mind declined;
and with their liberation of mind declined, they returned to that very bait set out by Māra and to those worldly baits.
There, intruding upon them and becoming infatuated, they ate their food.
While eating their food there, intruding and infatuated, they fell into intoxication; being intoxicated, they fell into negligence;
and being negligent, they became subject to Māra’s doing as he wished regarding that bait and that worldly lure.
"Thus indeed, even those second-order recluses and brahmins were not liberated from Māra’s power of psychic influence.
Suppose we were to establish our abode by relying on that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly baits;
having established our abode there, [we would rely] on that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly baits..."
‘We shall eat our food without intruding and without being infatuated; eating our food without intruding and without being infatuated, we shall not fall into intoxication;
being free from intoxication, we shall not fall into negligence;
being vigilant, we shall not become subject to Māra’s doing as he wishes regarding this sacrificial offering and this worldly bait.’”
Relying upon that bait set out by Māra and those worldly baits, they established their dwelling there.
Having established their dwelling there, they consumed their food without encroaching upon or becoming infatuated with that bait set out by Māra and those worldly baits.
Consuming their food there without encroaching or becoming infatuated, they did not fall into intoxication; being uninfatuated—
Being thus alike, they did not fall into negligence; being diligent, they did not become subject to Māra’s doing as he wished regarding that bait and that worldly lure.
However, they held such a view:
"The world is eternal," thus; "the world is non-eternal," thus;
"the world is finite," thus; "the world is infinite," thus;
"the soul and the body are the same," thus; "the soul is one thing and the body another," thus.

"The Tathāgata exists after death," "the Tathāgata does not exist after death," "the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death," or "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death.
In this way, monks, even these third class of recluses and brahmins were not liberated from the power and influence of Māra.
Monks, just as those third deer were, so do I describe these third recluses and brahmins.
In this regard, monks, the fourth recluses and brahmins reflected thus:
“Those first recluses and brahmins who [ate] that bait laid out by Māra...
In this way, those first recluses and brahmins were not liberated from the power of Māra’s psychic might.”
Then those second recluses and brahmins thought thus:
“As for those first recluses and brahmins… [as before]… Thus indeed those first recluses and brahmins were not liberated from Māra’s power of psychic influence.”
‘What if we were now to completely abstain from all bait-food and worldly baits, and, having abstained from these fearful enjoyments, enter and dwell in forest abodes?
They completely abstained from all bait-food and worldly baits… Thus, for a second time,
those ascetics and brahmins were not released from the power and influence of Māra.
Those third recluses and brahmins also thought thus: "As for those first recluses and brahmins... [and so on].
Thus indeed those first recluses and brahmins were not liberated from Māra’s power of psychic might.
Those second recluses and brahmins also thought thus: "As for those first recluses and brahmins... [and so on].
"In this way, those first ascetics and brahmins were not liberated from Māra’s supernatural power.
Suppose we were to abstain entirely from bait-food and worldly baits; being free from fear and enjoyment, let us enter deep into the forest dwellings and dwell there.
They abstained entirely from bait-food and worldly baits... [and so on]...
"Thus, even for a second time, those ascetics and brahmins were not liberated from Māra’s power of psychic influence.
Suppose we were to establish our dwelling by relying on that bait laid out by Māra and on those worldly baits.
Having established our dwelling there, without intruding upon that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly baits..."
"We shall eat food without being infatuated; eating food without being infatuated and without encroaching upon others, we shall not fall into intoxication;
being free from intoxication, we shall not fall into negligence;
and being vigilant, we shall not become subject to Māra’s doing as he pleases regarding that bait and that worldly lure."
Depending upon that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly baits, they established their dwelling there.
Having established their dwelling there, they consumed their food without encroaching upon or becoming infatuated with that bait laid out by Māra and those worldly baits.
Consuming their food there without encroaching or becoming infatuated, they did not fall into intoxication.
Being heedful, they did not fall into negligence.
Being heedful, they did not become subject to Māra’s doing as he wished regarding that bait and that worldly lure.
Rather, they held such views as: "The world is eternal," and so forth...
"Nor does the Tathāgata neither exist nor not exist after death"— thus,
these third class of recluses and brahmins were likewise not liberated from the power and influence of Māra.
"What if we were to establish our dwelling in that place where neither Māra nor Māra’s retinue can go?"
Having established our intention there, we shall partake of food without encroaching upon or becoming infatuated with that bait set out for Māra and these worldly pleasures;
by partaking of food without encroaching upon or becoming infatuated with them, we shall not fall into intoxication;
being un-intoxicated, we shall not fall into negligence; and being diligent, we shall not become subject to the doing of whatever they wish.
"We shall not fall into Māra’s trap at that bait and that worldly lure.
They established their dwelling in a place where neither Māra nor Māra’s retinue could go.
Having established their dwelling there, they remained without falling into that bait set out by Māra or those worldly lures.

They ate their food without being infatuated; eating there without encroaching upon others and without being infatuated, they did not fall into intoxication. Being uninfatuated, they did not fall into negligence.
Being diligent, they did not become subject to Māra’s doing as he wished regarding that bait and that worldly lure.
In this way, monks, those fourth recluses and brahmins were liberated from the power and influence of Māra.
Monks, just as those fourth species of deer, so do I describe these fourth recluses and brahmins.
And how, monks, is there no path for Māra or for Māra’s retinue?

"Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, who, having struck down Māra’s eye, has gone beyond the sight of the Evil One."

Furthermore, monks, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a monk enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is free from applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This, monks, is called [the destruction of the taints] … [up to] … by the Evil One.
Furthermore, monks, with the fading away of rapture, a monk dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
He experiences with the body that happiness of which the Noble Ones declare: "He dwells in happiness, mindful and equanimous";
thus he enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
This, monks, is called [the attainment of the stream-enterer]... [up to] ...of the Evil One.
Furthermore, monks, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a monk enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has escaped from the Evil One]...

Furthermore, monks, with the complete transcending of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory impact, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, thinking ‘space is infinite,’ a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite space.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has escaped from the Evil One]... [and so on].
Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite space, thinking "consciousness is infinite," a monk enters and dwells in the base of infinite consciousness.
This, monks, is called... [the attainment of one who has overcome] the Evil One.
Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing whatsoever," a monk enters and dwells in the base of nothingness.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has transcended the realm of Māra]…pe… of the Evil One.
Furthermore, monks, a monk, by completely surmounting the base of nothingness, enters and dwells in the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This, monks, is called [a monk who has transcended the realm of Māra]…pe… of the Evil One.

"Furthermore, monks, by completely transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, a monk enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. Having seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed.

This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, who has struck down Māra’s eye so that it finds no footing, and who has gone beyond the sight of the Evil One, having crossed over attachment to the world.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The fifth discourse, the Nivāpa Sutta, is concluded.
